subtype: Approach: assuming visitors will just arrive [Pitfall]
passage: In the school entrepreneurship club room, Trisha ma'am scrolled through Varun's finished site: a small online store for hand-poured candles, with careful photos and a tidy checkout page. It had taken him two weekends. “How many visitors so far?” she asked. Varun turned his laptop. The counter read 4, after three weeks. “Those are all my own refreshes,” he admitted. “Who did you tell?” “Nobody. People will find it. It's online.” Trisha ma'am didn't lecture. “Who lives near you? Who is in this room?” Varun looked at the forty candles in the box under the table. His shoulders sank. He had spent hours on the site and not one minute on telling a single person it existed.

qa.q: What did the visitor counter show?
qa.a: Four, all from Varun's own refreshes.

qa.q: What might Varun feel as he looks at the counter?
qa.a: Deflated and puzzled: he built the store carefully and nobody came.

qa.q: What could Varun do instead, and why?
qa.a: Tell classmates, neighbours and local groups about the store with a short message and flyers, since nobody visits a site they do not know exists.

qa.q: How does the store look to a classmate who never heard of it?
qa.a: It does not exist for that classmate at all, because nobody told them about it.

grounding: After finishing a small online store, a student waits for traffic and none comes because nobody was told.

subtype: Approach: assuming visitors will just arrive [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Samir bhai,
You asked how my online stall went. Honestly: badly, and it's my own fault.
I finished the site in May. Twenty hand-painted bookmarks, photos taken on the terrace in good light, a simple order form. I was so proud of it that I just waited. I thought people would find it, because it was online and anyone could see it.
Three weeks later, the visit counter said nine. Four of those were me checking.
I never told my class. I never showed the neighbourhood group or the aunties who run the Sunday craft fair. I spent all my planning on making it and none on telling anyone it existed. The bookmarks are still in a shoebox.
Could you tell me how you got the first customers for your tiffin service? I think I need to start there, not with a new design.
Farhan

qa.q: What did the visit counter say after three weeks?
qa.a: It said nine, and four of those were Farhan checking.

qa.q: How does Farhan seem to feel writing this letter?
qa.a: Farhan feels disappointed and a bit ashamed, calling it "my own fault", but also ready to learn 😔

qa.q: What could Farhan try first to find visitors?
qa.a: Tell the class, share the link in the neighbourhood group and ask to show the bookmarks at the Sunday craft fair, since people only come if they know.

qa.q: How might Samir bhai read this letter?
qa.a: Samir bhai may recognise a common first mistake and be glad Farhan is asking about customers rather than redesigning again.

grounding: Shows a student finishing a small online stall and waiting for visitors who never come, because there was no plan to tell anyone.

subtype: Approach: assuming visitors will just arrive [Pitfall]
passage:
You asked about my uniform-swap store, Binita, so okay, here's the embarrassing version. I'm Rashmi, the girl who built a whole online shop and then sat there waiting.
It was a good idea! Families outgrow uniforms every year, and new ones cost a lot. I photographed twenty sets, listed the sizes, and made a page to ask for one. It took the whole summer holiday. Then I launched it and... nothing. Week one, zero requests. Week two, one, from my own aunt, who felt sorry for me.
I kept refreshing the page as if people would just appear. They didn't, because nobody knew it existed. I never put up a notice at school, never asked the parents' group, never told the tailor near the gate who sees every family in June.
Next June I'm doing the telling part first, before I take a single photo.

qa.q: How many requests came in during week one?
How does Rashmi feel looking back on all that refreshing?
qa.a: Rashmi feels embarrassed about it, calling it the embarrassing version, though the plan for next June sounds hopeful.

qa.q: What else could Rashmi do next June besides a notice at school?
qa.a: Ask the tailor near the gate to mention the page, since that tailor sees every family in June.

qa.q: How might Binita react to hearing this story?
qa.a: Binita may find it funny and familiar, and might offer to spread the word next June.

grounding: Shows a student finishing an online uniform shop and waiting for traffic that never comes, because no plan existed for telling people.
